design.quote: Semi-structured one-to-one interviews were conducted with 20 adults who currently or previously used heroin (for at least 6 months), with any type of administration (injected, smoked) and experience of abstinence (at least 2 weeks) and relapse.
design.text: A qualitative study of 20 adults who currently or previously used heroin.

findings.where: Results › “As time went by my tolerance got higher and [I] started using higher and bigger amounts”: Tolerating tolerance › Inevitability and frustration
findings.quote: When using regularly, many described tolerance to the desired effects as inevitably increasing over time (a few days to two years) depending on frequency of use.
findings.text: Many people who use heroin report that tolerance to the desired effects of the drug inevitably increases over time when using regularly.

findings.quote: We report the first qualitative evidence of tolerance to the psychoactive effects of heroin developing more quickly with each relapse episode.
findings.text: There is evidence that tolerance to the psychoactive effects of heroin develops more quickly with each episode of relapse.

findings.where: Results › “As time went by my tolerance got higher and [I] started using higher and bigger amounts”: Tolerating tolerance › Inevitability and frustration
findings.quote: After long periods of using heroin, the ‘high’ diminished completely; instead, using was necessary to feel ‘normal’ and remove withdrawal symptoms
findings.text: After long periods of use, the high from heroin can diminish completely, making the drug necessary to feel normal and avoid withdrawal symptoms.

limits.quote: Whether rapid tolerance is perceived to develop after abstinence and re-exposure to prescription opioids such as oxycodone, and to the fentanyls remains to be determined.
limits.text: It is not yet determined if rapid tolerance develops after abstinence and re-exposure to prescription opioids like oxycodone or to fentanyls.

findings.quote: Increased tolerance was particularly true for participants who used heroin to supplement their medical or nonmedical use, as heroin quality and strength varied considerably

limits.quote: Although our participants do not represent the majority who were prescribed opioids for pain, most of whom take them only as prescribed and do not switch to heroin, the increasing rates of overdose deaths due to heroin and fentanyl suggests that the number of people who switched to heroin is not trivial.

findings.quote: Regular use may eventually contribute to: intense sadness; irregular periods and difficulty having children; no sex drive, erectile dysfunction and infertility in men; constipation; dental issues; damaged heart, lungs, liver and brain; vein damage and skin, heart and lung infections from injecting; needing to use more to get the same effect; dependence on heroin.
findings.text: Regular use of heroin may eventually contribute to needing to use more to get the same effect.

findings.quote: Tolerance to heroin also affects other opioids (known as cross-tolerance). For example, tolerance to heroin will also result in a higher tolerance to oxycodone or fentanyl.
